chunks: The idolaters will say: 'If God had so willed, we would not have associated (others with Him), nor would our fathers, nor would we have forbidden anything.' So it was with those who denied before them, until they tasted Our punishment. Ask them: 'Do you have any knowledge, then produce it? You follow nothing but conjecture, and you are nothing but liars.'

key_terms.أَشْرَكُوا: Idolaters / those who associated partners with God

ai.seo_question: What is the argument of the polytheists regarding divine will, and how does the Quran refute it?
ai.summary: In Shia exegesis, this verse highlights the polytheists' use of 'divine will' (mashī'ah) as a rhetorical shield to excuse their deviation, a theme echoed in the concept of divine justice where will does not negate accountability. The challenge to produce 'knowledge' (ʿilm) contrasts their baseless conjecture (ẓann) with the definitive revelation received by the Imams and Prophets. This underscores the Shia emphasis on rational proof and transmitted tradition over mere ancestral custom or speculative belief.
